subject: physics

items.q: Carbon-12 (¹²₆C) and carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C) are isotopes of carbon. Which statement about these two nuclides is correct?
items.correct: Both contain the same number of protons, but different numbers of neutrons.
items.misconception: They contain the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons.
items.why: Two numbers are written beside the symbol and the nucleus contains two kinds of particle, so it seems natural that each number counts one kind. The older labels 'mass number' and 'atomic number' do not say which particles are counted, and neither number is the neutron number. The upper number A counts all the nucleons, protons and neutrons together; the lower number Z counts protons only. The neutron number is found by subtraction, N = A − Z. All isotopes of carbon have Z = 6 and differ only in A.
items.specStatementText: isotopes
items.random_wrong: Their atoms have different chemical properties, as their nuclei differ.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the binding energy of a nucleus?
items.correct: The minimum energy needed to pull the nucleus apart into separate nucleons.
items.misconception: The energy released when the nucleus is separated completely into its nucleons.
items.why: The belief that breaking chemical bonds releases energy is widespread among chemistry students (fuels 'release energy when they burn'), and it is carried over to the 'bonds' in a nucleus. The phrase 'binding energy' also sounds like energy that the nucleus holds and can give out. Nucleons attract one another through the strong nuclear force, so work must be done to pull them apart. The binding energy is the minimum energy needed to separate the nucleus completely into its nucleons. Energy is released when a nucleus FORMS; energy must be supplied to take it apart.
items.specStatementText: nuclear binding energy and mass defect
items.random_wrong: The energy stored inside the nucleus, which it gives out when it later decays.

items.q: The masses of a proton, a neutron and a helium-4 nucleus (⁴₂He) are 938.27 MeV c⁻², 939.57 MeV c⁻² and 3727.38 MeV c⁻² respectively. What is the binding energy per nucleon of helium-4?
items.why:
Both quantities are called 'binding energy' in conversation and appear side by side in tables and graphs. Students remember that 'more binding energy means more stable' and drop the words 'per nucleon'. To compare how tightly nuclei are bound, divide the total binding energy by the nucleon number. The binding energy curve plots binding energy per nucleon, and the nuclei near its peak are the most tightly bound. Energy is released when nuclei change into nuclei with a greater binding energy per nucleon.

Working: Mass defect Δm = 2m_p + 2m_n − m_He = 2(938.27) + 2(939.57) − 3727.38 = 3755.68 − 3727.38 = 28.30 MeV c⁻². Binding energy E_b = Δmc² = 28.30 MeV. Helium-4 has A = 4 nucleons, so E_b/A = 28.30 MeV/4 = 7.075 MeV.
items.specStatementText: nuclear binding energy and mass defect
items.working: Mass defect Δm = 2m_p + 2m_n − m_He = 2(938.27) + 2(939.57) − 3727.38 = 3755.68 − 3727.38 = 28.30 MeV c⁻². Binding energy E_b = Δmc² = 28.30 MeV. Helium-4 has A = 4 nucleons, so E_b/A = 28.30 MeV/4 = 7.075 MeV.

items.q: Approximate binding energies per nucleon are: ²₁H 1.1 MeV; ⁴₂He 7.1 MeV; ²⁸₁₄Si 8.4 MeV; ⁵⁶₂₆Fe 8.8 MeV; ¹¹⁸₅₀Sn 8.5 MeV; ²³⁶₉₂U 7.6 MeV. Which of these processes would release energy?
items.correct: Fusing two ²₁H nuclei to form one ⁴₂He nucleus
items.misconception: Splitting one ⁵⁶₂₆Fe nucleus into two ²⁸₁₄Si nuclei
items.why:
Fission and fusion are met as the two sources of nuclear energy, in reactors and in the Sun, so each process is associated with energy release rather than with where the nuclei lie on the binding energy curve. Read the binding energy per nucleon curve: a reaction releases energy if the products lie higher on the curve than the reactants. Light nuclei move up the curve by fusing and heavy nuclei by splitting; nuclei near the peak (A ≈ 56–62) cannot release energy by either process.

Working: Energy is released if the total binding energy (A × binding energy per nucleon) increases. 2 ²H → ⁴He: 4(7.1) − 2 × 2(1.1) = 28.4 − 4.4 = +24 MeV (released). ⁵⁶Fe → 2 ²⁸Si: 56(8.4) − 56(8.8) = −22 MeV (must be supplied). 2 ¹¹⁸Sn → ²³⁶U: 236(7.6) − 236(8.5) = −212 MeV (must be supplied). ⁴He → 4 free nucleons: 0 − 4(7.1) = −28 MeV (must be supplied).
items.specStatementText: the variation of the binding energy per nucleon with nucleon number
items.random_wrong: Joining two ¹¹⁸₅₀Sn nuclei into one ²³⁶₉₂U nucleus
items.working: Energy is released if the total binding energy (A × binding energy per nucleon) increases. 2 ²H → ⁴He: 4(7.1) − 2 × 2(1.1) = 28.4 − 4.4 = +24 MeV (released). ⁵⁶Fe → 2 ²⁸Si: 56(8.4) − 56(8.8) = −22 MeV (must be supplied). 2 ¹¹⁸Sn → ²³⁶U: 236(7.6) − 236(8.5) = −212 MeV (must be supplied). ⁴He → 4 free nucleons: 0 − 4(7.1) = −28 MeV (must be supplied).

items.q: In the fusion reaction ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n, the binding energies per nucleon are 1.11 MeV for ²₁H, 2.83 MeV for ³₁H and 7.07 MeV for ⁴₂He. A free neutron has no binding energy. How much energy is released in one reaction?
items.correct: 17.6 MeV
items.misconception: 10.7 MeV
items.why:
The word 'energy' in 'binding energy' is read as a store that the nucleus possesses, like the chemical energy in a fuel. Nuclear power is often described as 'releasing the energy in the nucleus', which reinforces the idea. Binding energy measures how much energy it would take to pull the nucleus apart, so more binding energy means a more tightly bound nucleus. The energy released in a nuclear reaction equals the INCREASE in total binding energy from reactants to products (equivalently, the decrease in rest mass multiplied by c²), not the binding energy of any one nucleus.

Working: Total binding energy = A × (binding energy per nucleon). Reactants: ²H: 2 × 1.11 = 2.22 MeV; ³H: 3 × 2.83 = 8.49 MeV; total 10.71 MeV. Products: ⁴He: 4 × 7.07 = 28.28 MeV; neutron 0. Energy released = 28.28 MeV − 10.71 MeV = 17.57 MeV ≈ 17.6 MeV.
items.specStatementText: the variation of the binding energy per nucleon with nucleon number
items.random_wrong: 28.3 MeV
items.working: Total binding energy = A × (binding energy per nucleon). Reactants: ²H: 2 × 1.11 = 2.22 MeV; ³H: 3 × 2.83 = 8.49 MeV; total 10.71 MeV. Products: ⁴He: 4 × 7.07 = 28.28 MeV; neutron 0. Energy released = 28.28 MeV − 10.71 MeV = 17.57 MeV ≈ 17.6 MeV.

items.q: Radium-226 decays by α emission: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂α. The atomic masses are 226.025410 u for radium-226, 222.017578 u for radon-222 and 4.002603 u for helium-4 (the electron masses cancel). Take 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV c⁻², 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. How much energy is released in the decay of one radium-226 nucleus?
items.why:
A procedural slip, made more likely because c is a familiar number and the index is easily lost in handwriting. Students who do not check units do not notice that kg × m s⁻¹ is not a unit of energy. Use E = mc² with c² = (3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)² = 9.00 × 10¹⁶ m² s⁻², and check the unit: kg m² s⁻² = J.

Working: Δm = m(Ra) − [m(Rn) + m(He)] = 226.025410 u − (222.017578 u + 4.002603 u) = 0.005229 u = 0.005229 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 8.685 × 10⁻³⁰ kg. E = Δmc² = 8.685 × 10⁻³⁰ kg × (3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)² = 7.82 × 10⁻¹³ J ≈ 7.8 × 10⁻¹³ J. Check in MeV: 0.005229 u × 931.5 MeV u⁻¹ = 4.87 MeV = 4.87 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J = 7.79 × 10⁻¹³ J ≈ 7.8 × 10⁻¹³ J.
items.specStatementText: the mass-energy equivalence as given by E = mc² in nuclear reactions

items.q: Nucleons in a nucleus are about 10⁻¹⁵ m apart, while the nuclei of neighbouring atoms in a solid are about 10⁻¹⁰ m apart. Why does the strong nuclear force bind the nucleons within each nucleus but have no effect between neighbouring nuclei?
items.correct: Its range is so short that it is negligible at separations much above 10⁻¹⁵ m.
items.misconception: It is a repulsive force between nuclei, as every nucleus carries positive charge.
items.why:
The only forces students have met inside atoms are electric ones, and the strong force is introduced alongside the repulsion between protons, so it is taken to be a stronger version of the same kind of force. The strong nuclear force is a separate interaction. It attracts any two nucleons about 10⁻¹⁵ m apart, whatever their charge, and it does not act on electrons at all. It is not felt between neighbouring nuclei because of its very short range, not because of their charge.

Working: The strong nuclear force acts only over distances of the order of 10⁻¹⁵ m. Neighbouring nuclei in a solid are about 10⁻¹⁰ m apart, 10⁵ times further, where the strong force is negligible.
items.specStatementText: the existence of the strong nuclear force, a short-range, attractive force between nucleons
items.random_wrong: The electrons around each nucleus block the force from reaching other nuclei.
items.working: The strong nuclear force acts only over distances of the order of 10⁻¹⁵ m. Neighbouring nuclei in a solid are about 10⁻¹⁰ m apart, 10⁵ times further, where the strong force is negligible.

items.q: Radioactive decay is described as random and spontaneous. Which statement correctly describes what this means?
items.correct: When a given nucleus decays cannot be predicted, and outside conditions do not alter its chance.
items.misconception: A nucleus decays when a collision or a rise in temperature gives it the energy it needs.
items.why: Almost every other change students study (chemical reactions, melting, evaporation) goes faster at higher temperature or needs a trigger, so students expect nuclear decay to behave in the same way. Research on students' ideas about radioactivity reports this belief. The energies involved in heating or in chemical change (at most a few eV per atom) are tiny compared with nuclear energies (MeV). Decay depends on the nucleus, and each nucleus has a fixed chance of decaying in a given time that ordinary physical and chemical conditions do not change.
items.specStatementText: the random and spontaneous nature of radioactive decay
items.random_wrong: Nuclei decay roughly in the order in which they formed, but their ages cannot be known.

items.q: Radon-222 has a half-life of 3.8 days. A particular radon-222 nucleus in a sample has not decayed after 3.8 days. What is the probability that this nucleus decays during the next 3.8 days?
items.correct: ½, the same as for any other undecayed radon-222 nucleus
items.misconception: Greater than ½ but less than 1, as it has survived one half-life
items.why:
Everyday objects wear out and living things die of old age, so students expect nuclei to have a lifetime after which they decay. The gambler's fallacy, that a long run without an event makes it more likely next time, strengthens the idea. Radioactive decay is random: the chance that an undecayed nucleus decays in the next interval does not depend on its past. After one half-life the surviving nuclei are exactly like new nuclei of the same nuclide, and each still has a chance of ½ of decaying in the next half-life.

Working: 3.8 days is one half-life. The nucleus has survived one half-life, but nuclei do not age: the probability that any undecayed radon-222 nucleus decays within the next half-life is ½, so P = ½.
items.specStatementText: the random and spontaneous nature of radioactive decay
items.random_wrong: 1, since radon-222 decays completely in two half-lives
items.working: 3.8 days is one half-life. The nucleus has survived one half-life, but nuclei do not age: the probability that any undecayed radon-222 nucleus decays within the next half-life is ½, so P = ½.

items.q: A nucleus X undergoes α decay. The daughter nucleus then undergoes two β⁻ decays in succession. How does the final nucleus compare with X?
items.correct: It is an isotope of X whose nucleus has four fewer neutrons than X.
items.misconception: It is an isotope of X whose nucleus has six fewer neutrons than X.
items.why:
Students learn that α emission removes 4 nucleons and generalize that every emitted particle takes some nucleons with it. The difference between a nucleon and an electron is lost. Write the β particle with its nucleon number, ⁰₋₁e or ⁰₊₁e. Because its nucleon number is 0, balancing the equation shows that A is the same before and after the decay.

Working: α decay: Z − 2, N − 2 (A − 4). Each β⁻ decay: a neutron becomes a proton, so Z + 1 and N − 1 (A unchanged). Overall: Z − 2 + 1 + 1 = Z (same element); N − 2 − 1 − 1 = N − 4; A − 4. The final nucleus is an isotope of X with 4 fewer neutrons.
items.specStatementText: the changes in the state of the nucleus following alpha, beta and gamma radioactive decay
items.random_wrong: It is another element, with two fewer protons and two fewer neutrons.
items.working: α decay: Z − 2, N − 2 (A − 4). Each β⁻ decay: a neutron becomes a proton, so Z + 1 and N − 1 (A unchanged). Overall: Z − 2 + 1 + 1 = Z (same element); N − 2 − 1 − 1 = N − 4; A − 4. The final nucleus is an isotope of X with 4 fewer neutrons.

items.q: Which of these radioactive decay equations is correct?
items.correct: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂α
items.misconception: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e + ⁰₀ν
items.why:
Students try to pair like with like: the positron is an antiparticle, so it seems it should come with the antiparticle ν̄, leaving the ordinary neutrino for β⁻ decay. The pairing is matter with antimatter: the electron (matter) is emitted with an antineutrino (antimatter), and the positron (antimatter) with a neutrino (matter): n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ and p → n + e⁺ + ν.

Working: Check each equation for conservation of nucleon number and charge, and for the right particles. α: 226 = 222 + 4 and 88 = 86 + 2, correct. β⁻ (carbon-14): the numbers balance, but β⁻ decay emits an antineutrino, ⁰₀ν̄, not a neutrino. β⁺ (fluorine-18): charge 9 ≠ 10 + 1; the daughter is ¹⁸₈O. γ: charge 56 ≠ 55 + 0; γ emission leaves the nuclide as ¹³⁷₅₆Ba.
items.specStatementText: the radioactive decay equations involving α, β⁻, β⁺, γ
items.random_wrong: ¹⁸₉F → ¹⁸₁₀Ne + ⁰₊₁e + ⁰₀ν

items.q: The four decays below involve nuclides used in medicine and industry. Which decay equation is correct?
items.correct: ¹³¹₅₃I → ¹³¹₅₄Xe + ⁰₋₁e + ⁰₀ν̄
items.misconception: ²⁴¹₉₅Am → ²³⁷₉₃Np + ⁴₂α + ⁰₀ν
items.why:
Having learned that a β decay equation must include a neutrino or antineutrino, students overgeneralize and add one to every decay equation as part of the pattern of writing a decay. Include ⁰₀ν only with β⁺ decay and ⁰₀ν̄ only with β⁻ decay. An α decay equation contains only the parent, the daughter and the α particle; a γ emission contains only the nucleus and the photon.

Working: Iodine-131 (β⁻): 131 = 131 + 0 + 0 and 53 = 54 − 1 + 0, with an antineutrino as required: correct. Americium-241 (α): the numbers balance, but α decay emits no neutrino. Fluorine-18 (β⁺): the numbers balance, but β⁺ decay emits a neutrino, not an antineutrino. Strontium-90 (β⁻): charge balances (38 = 39 − 1) but nucleon number does not (90 ≠ 89 + 0); the daughter is ⁹⁰₃₉Y.

items.q: An electron antineutrino, ν̄, is emitted in every β⁻ decay. Which statement about the antineutrino is correct?
items.correct: It is uncharged, has a very small mass and very rarely interacts with matter.
items.misconception: It is a neutron that leaves the nucleus together with the β⁻ particle.
items.why: The names sound alike ('neutr-' for neutral) and both particles are uncharged, so students assume they are the same particle or closely related. In β⁻ decay a neutron is used up, not emitted: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄. The antineutrino has nucleon number 0, which is why it is written ⁰₀ν̄ in decay equations.
items.specStatementText: the existence of neutrinos ν and antineutrinos ν̄
items.random_wrong: It is positively charged, balancing the negative charge of the β⁻ particle.

items.q: Technetium-99m emits γ rays only and has a half-life of 6.0 h. It is injected into patients so that the organs that take it up can be imaged by a γ camera outside the body. Which statement is a correct reason for choosing technetium-99m?
items.correct: Its γ rays are weakly ionizing and most pass out of the body to the camera.
items.misconception: Its γ rays are strongly ionizing, so they give a strong signal at the camera.
items.why: Students rank radiation by a single idea of 'strength' or danger. γ rays are described as 'the most dangerous' and 'high energy', and α particles as 'heavy and powerful', so either may be credited with every property. Each ionization takes energy from the radiation. α particles ionize densely, so they give up their energy within a few centimetres of air; γ photons ionize rarely, so they travel far. Choose radiation for a use by matching its penetration to the job.
items.specStatementText: the penetration and ionizing ability of alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays
items.random_wrong: Its half-life is short because so little is injected, and a small sample halves quickly.

items.q: A small amount of sodium-24 (half-life 15 h), which emits β⁻ particles and γ rays, is added to water flowing in a pipe buried 1 m underground. A detector moved along the surface above the pipe records a much higher count rate above one point. Which statement explains this reading?
items.correct: γ rays from the tracer that has leaked into the soil pass up through the ground.
items.misconception: β⁻ particles from the leaked tracer have the energy to cross a metre of soil.
items.why: β particles are described as 'more penetrating than α', and students stretch 'more penetrating' to 'very penetrating' without a sense of scale: a few millimetres of aluminium compared with several centimetres of lead. Learn the ranges with numbers: α, a sheet of paper or a few cm of air; β, a few mm of aluminium; γ, reduced significantly only by several cm of lead or thick concrete. Radiation that must pass through soil, tissue or walls must be γ.
items.specStatementText: the penetration and ionizing ability of alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays
items.random_wrong: The tracer decays faster once it is out of the pipe, so it emits more there.

items.q: A paper mill monitors the thickness of its paper, about 0.1 mm thick, with a radioactive source above the moving paper and a detector below it. The count rate is used to adjust the rollers. Which type of source is most suitable, and why?
items.correct: β⁻, as the paper absorbs part of the β⁻ radiation, and more when it is thicker.
items.misconception: γ, as γ rays pass through the paper easily and so give a high count rate.
items.why: Students reason that the detector needs to receive plenty of radiation and that more counts give a better measurement; they do not consider that the reading must CHANGE when the thickness changes. The gauge works through the change in count rate. Choose radiation that the material absorbs significantly but not completely: β for paper, plastic and thin metal foil; γ for thick steel.
items.specStatementText: the penetration and ionizing ability of alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays
items.random_wrong: α, as α particles are the most ionizing and also the most penetrating radiation.

items.q: Sealed packs of surgical instruments are sterilized by exposing them to intense γ radiation from a cobalt-60 source, which kills bacteria. Which statement about this process is correct?
items.correct: The instruments do not become radioactive: they are irradiated, not contaminated.
items.misconception: The instruments become radioactive and must be stored until their activity has fallen.
items.why: Research on students' ideas about radioactivity has repeatedly found that 'radiation' and 'radioactive material' are not distinguished, so exposure to radiation is thought to pass on radioactivity, as touching dirt makes things dirty. Everyday phrases such as 'contaminated by radiation' reinforce this. Distinguish irradiation (exposure to radiation from a source outside the object) from contamination (radioactive material getting onto or into the object). An irradiated object stops being exposed the moment the source is removed and emits nothing itself; a contaminated object keeps emitting until the material is removed or decays.
items.specStatementText: the penetration and ionizing ability of alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays
items.random_wrong: Some of the γ radiation stays trapped inside each sealed pack until the pack is opened.

items.q: Cobalt-60 has a half-life of 5.3 years and decays into nickel-60, a stable solid. A sample contains a large number of cobalt-60 nuclei. Which statement about the sample is correct?
items.correct: After 5.3 years, about half of the cobalt-60 nuclei present now will remain.
items.misconception: After 10.6 years, all of the cobalt-60 nuclei will have decayed.
items.why:
The word 'half-life' suggests half of a lifetime, and students picture a sample as having a total lifetime, like a candle burning down at a steady rate. Research on students' understanding of half-life reports this interpretation as common. Half-life is the time for the number of undecayed nuclei (or the activity) to fall to half. It is the same for every halving: N₀ to N₀/2, N₀/2 to N₀/4, and so on. After n half-lives the fraction remaining is (½)ⁿ.

Working: Half-life is the time for the number of undecayed nuclei to halve: after 5.3 years N = N₀/2; after 10.6 years (two half-lives) N = N₀/4, not zero.
items.specStatementText: the activity, count rate and half-life in radioactive decay
items.random_wrong: After 5.3 years, the sample's mass will be about half of its mass now.
items.working: Half-life is the time for the number of undecayed nuclei to halve: after 5.3 years N = N₀/2; after 10.6 years (two half-lives) N = N₀/4, not zero.

items.q: To determine the half-life of a nuclide, a student measures the count rate from a sample and the background count rate. After subtracting the background, the count rate falls from 640 counts s⁻¹ at t = 0 to 80 counts s⁻¹ at t = 120 min. What is the half-life of the nuclide?
items.correct: 40 min
items.misconception: 69 min
items.why:
A steady, linear change is the default model students use for anything that decreases, and a straight line is the easiest way to interpolate between two data points. Look at a table of values: 800, 400, 200, 100 at equal time intervals. The falls are 400, 200 and 100, not constant; the ratio of successive values is constant. Use halving, not subtraction, to find how the activity changes.

Working: 640/80 = 8 = 2³, so the corrected count rate has halved three times: 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 counts s⁻¹. Three half-lives = 120 min, so T½ = 120 min/3 = 40 min.
items.specStatementText: the activity, count rate and half-life in radioactive decay
items.random_wrong: 15 min
items.working: 640/80 = 8 = 2³, so the corrected count rate has halved three times: 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 counts s⁻¹. Three half-lives = 120 min, so T½ = 120 min/3 = 40 min.

items.q: A hospital prepares a dose of technetium-99m (half-life 6.0 h) that has an activity of 800 MBq at 08:00. What will its activity be at 14:00 the next day?
items.correct: 25 MBq
items.misconception: 160 MBq
items.why:
Students confuse repeated halving with a single division by the number of steps. This is a general difficulty with repeated multiplication (powers) rather than a specific physics idea, and it survives because the first case, one half-life and a factor of 2, gives no warning. Halve step by step, or use (½)ⁿ: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 after 4 half-lives, which is 800/2⁴. To find n from a factor, count halvings or solve 2ⁿ = factor: 8 = 2³, so n = 3.

Working: From 08:00 to 14:00 the next day is 30 h = 30 h/6.0 h = 5 half-lives. A = 800 MBq × (½)⁵ = 800 MBq/32 = 25 MBq.
items.specStatementText: the changes in activity and count rate during radioactive decay using integer values of half-life
items.random_wrong: 0 MBq
items.working: From 08:00 to 14:00 the next day is 30 h = 30 h/6.0 h = 5 half-lives. A = 800 MBq × (½)⁵ = 800 MBq/32 = 25 MBq.

items.q: Carbon-14 (half-life 5730 years) is used to date wood. Equal masses of carbon from a living tree and from an ancient wooden tool give background-corrected count rates of 96 and 12 counts per minute. Assuming that the proportion of carbon-14 in living wood has not changed, how old is the tool?
items.why:
A counting ('fencepost') error: students count the numbers they have written down, or the clock times they have listed, rather than the steps between them. Count the arrows, not the numbers: 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 has three arrows, so three half-lives. Check with time: at t = 0 no half-lives have passed.

Working: 96/12 = 8 = 2³, so three half-lives have passed: 96 → 48 → 24 → 12 counts per minute. Age = 3 × 5730 y = 17 190 y ≈ 1.72 × 10⁴ y.
items.specStatementText: the changes in activity and count rate during radioactive decay using integer values of half-life
items.working: 96/12 = 8 = 2³, so three half-lives have passed: 96 → 48 → 24 → 12 counts per minute. Age = 3 × 5730 y = 17 190 y ≈ 1.72 × 10⁴ y.

items.q: A detector placed near a source of half-life 2.0 days records 250 counts min⁻¹. With the source removed, it records a background of 50 counts min⁻¹. What will the detector record with the source in the same place 6.0 days later?
items.correct: 75 counts min⁻¹
items.misconception: 31 counts min⁻¹
items.why:
Students see a single reading on the counter and treat all of it as coming from the source; separating the reading into contributions is not automatic. Measure the background with the source removed, subtract it from every reading to get the corrected count rate, apply the halving to the corrected value, and add the background back to predict what the counter will show.

Working: Corrected count rate now = 250 − 50 = 200 counts min⁻¹. 6.0 days = 3 half-lives, so the corrected count rate becomes 200/2³ = 25 counts min⁻¹. Measured count rate = 25 + 50 = 75 counts min⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: the effect of background radiation on count rate.
items.random_wrong: 25 counts min⁻¹
items.working: Corrected count rate now = 250 − 50 = 200 counts min⁻¹. 6.0 days = 3 half-lives, so the corrected count rate becomes 200/2³ = 25 counts min⁻¹. Measured count rate = 25 + 50 = 75 counts min⁻¹.

items.q: In a helium-4 nucleus the two protons are about 2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m apart. At this separation the electric repulsion between them is about 58 N, an enormous force on particles of mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Yet helium-4 nuclei are stable. What does this evidence show?
items.correct: An attraction stronger than the electric repulsion must act between nucleons.
items.misconception: Gravitational attraction between protons this close together balances the repulsion.
items.why: Students know that gravity increases as masses get closer and that gravity holds planets and stars together, so it is a natural candidate for the attraction in a nucleus. They do not estimate how small the masses of nucleons are. Estimate both forces for two protons in a nucleus: Gm²/r² ≈ 10⁻³⁵ N and ke²/r² ≈ 60 N. Gravity cannot balance the repulsion; a far stronger attraction between nucleons, the strong nuclear force, is needed.
items.specStatementText: the evidence for the strong nuclear force
items.random_wrong: The neutrons attract the protons, but the two protons exert no attraction on each other.

items.q: The stable isotopes of carbon are ¹²₆C and ¹³₆C. Carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C) is radioactive. Which decay does carbon-14 undergo, and why?
items.correct: β⁻ decay, as a neutron changes into a proton and lowers its N/Z ratio
items.misconception: β⁺ decay, as this turns one of its surplus neutrons into a proton
items.why: Students link the minus sign of β⁻ with a decrease ('minus' means 'take away') and the plus sign of β⁺ with an increase, and skip the charge-balance reasoning. Use conservation of charge. In β⁻ decay a negative particle leaves, so the nucleus must become more positive: a neutron becomes a proton and Z rises by 1. In β⁺ decay a positive particle leaves, so a proton becomes a neutron and Z falls by 1.
items.specStatementText: the role of the ratio of neutrons to protons for the stability of nuclides
items.random_wrong: α decay, as the α particle carries two of its surplus neutrons away with it

items.q: For nuclides with nucleon number A above about 60, the binding energy per nucleon changes very little, staying between about 7.6 MeV and 8.8 MeV. What does this suggest about the strong nuclear force?
items.correct: Each nucleon is attracted only by its nearest neighbours, as the force has a very short range.
items.misconception: Each nucleon attracts every other nucleon in the nucleus, as the force has a long range.
items.why: Gravitational and electric forces are both taught as inverse-square forces with unlimited range, and students generalize that pattern to every force they meet. If the strong force fell off as 1/r² like the electric force, it would stay far stronger than the electric repulsion at every separation, and neighbouring nuclei in a solid would be pulled together. They are not: the strong force acts only between nucleons that are very close together.
items.specStatementText: the approximate constancy of binding energy curve above a nucleon number of 60
items.random_wrong: It gives every nucleus with A above 60 about the same total binding energy.

items.q: Almost all the α particles emitted by radium-226 have one of two energies, 4.78 MeV or 4.60 MeV. The daughter nucleus, radon-222, emits γ photons of energy 0.19 MeV. (The α energies differ by slightly less than 0.19 MeV because the recoiling radon nucleus takes a small share of the energy.) Which conclusion do these observations support?
items.correct: Radon-222 has discrete energy levels, one of them 0.19 MeV above its ground state.
items.misconception: The radium sample is a mixture of two isotopes, each emitting α particles of one energy.
items.why:
Students learn one characteristic α energy for each nuclide (usually the most common one) and treat that energy as a fingerprint that must be unique. Discrete nuclear energy levels explain the pattern: radium-226 decays either to the ground state of radon-222 (α energy 4.78 MeV) or to an excited state 0.19 MeV above it (α energy 4.60 MeV), and the excited radon nucleus then emits a 0.19 MeV γ photon.

Working: Difference in α energies = 4.78 MeV − 4.60 MeV = 0.18 MeV, which matches the 0.19 MeV γ photon once the small recoil energy of the radon nucleus is allowed for. So one α decay mode leaves radon-222 in an excited state about 0.19 MeV above its ground state, from which it emits the γ photon: evidence for discrete nuclear energy levels.
items.specStatementText: that the spectrum of alpha and gamma radiations provides evidence for discrete nuclear energy levels
items.random_wrong: The γ photons come from electrons of the radon atom falling between atomic energy levels.
items.working: Difference in α energies = 4.78 MeV − 4.60 MeV = 0.18 MeV, which matches the 0.19 MeV γ photon once the small recoil energy of the radon nucleus is allowed for. So one α decay mode leaves radon-222 in an excited state about 0.19 MeV above its ground state, from which it emits the γ photon: evidence for discrete nuclear energy levels.

items.q: In the β⁻ decay of a particular nuclide, the emitted electrons have a continuous range of kinetic energies, from almost zero up to a maximum value. Which statement correctly explains this?
items.correct: The energy released is shared in varying proportions between the electron and an antineutrino.
items.misconception: Electrons lose different amounts of energy in collisions with atoms before they leave the source.
items.why: Students know that β particles lose energy by ionizing atoms, so energy loss inside the source seems a natural explanation for a spread, and it avoids the need for an unseen particle. If a decay produced only two bodies (the electron and the daughter nucleus), conservation of energy and momentum would give the electron one definite energy, as for α particles. A continuous spread from one nuclear transition therefore needs a third particle to carry away the rest of the energy: the antineutrino.
items.specStatementText: the continuous spectrum of beta decay as evidence for the neutrino
items.random_wrong: The electrons come from different shells of the atom, which have different binding energies.

items.q: The activity per gram of carbon in a sample of bone is 23% of that in living tissue. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. Assuming the proportion of carbon-14 in living tissue has not changed, what is the age of the bone?
items.why:
Both quantities describe how quickly decay happens and they have reciprocal units (s and s⁻¹), so students assume they are simple reciprocals, as frequency and time period are. Put N = N₀/2 into N = N₀e^(−λt): ½ = e^(−λT½), so λT½ = ln 2 and T½ = ln 2/λ. Always include the factor ln 2 = 0.693.

Working: A = A₀e^(−λt) with A/A₀ = 0.23. λ = ln 2/T½ = 0.693/5730 y = 1.210 × 10⁻⁴ y⁻¹. t = ln(A₀/A)/λ = ln(1/0.23)/(1.210 × 10⁻⁴ y⁻¹) = 1.470/(1.210 × 10⁻⁴ y⁻¹) = 1.21 × 10⁴ y ≈ 1.2 × 10⁴ y.
items.specStatementText: the decay constant λ and the radioactive decay law as given by N = N₀e^(−λt)

items.q: A nuclide has a decay constant λ = 0.10 s⁻¹. What is the probability that a particular undecayed nucleus of this nuclide decays within the next 5.0 s?
items.why:
λ is often introduced as 'the probability of decay per unit time', and multiplying a rate by a time to get a total is a habit from uniform-rate problems. The condition that λt must be small is easily forgotten. The probability of surviving for time t is e^(−λt), so the probability of decaying is 1 − e^(−λt) ≈ λt only for small λt. For larger λt the approximation overestimates, and λt can even exceed 1, which no probability can.

Working: Probability of surviving for t = 5.0 s: e^(−λt) = e^(−0.10 s⁻¹ × 5.0 s) = e^(−0.50) = 0.607. Probability of decaying = 1 − 0.607 = 0.393 ≈ 0.39. (λt = 0.50 is not small, so the approximation P ≈ λt = 0.50 is poor.)
items.specStatementText: that the decay constant approximates the probability of decay in unit time only in the limit of sufficiently small λt
items.working: Probability of surviving for t = 5.0 s: e^(−λt) = e^(−0.10 s⁻¹ × 5.0 s) = e^(−0.50) = 0.607. Probability of decaying = 1 − 0.607 = 0.393 ≈ 0.39. (λt = 0.50 is not small, so the approximation P ≈ λt = 0.50 is poor.)

items.q: Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8.0 days and a molar mass of 131 g mol⁻¹. What is the activity of 1.0 μg of iodine-131? Take N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ and 1 day = 8.64 × 10⁴ s.
items.why:
Physics teaching rightly insists on SI units, so students convert every mass to kg automatically, but molar masses are usually quoted in g mol⁻¹ and the matching conversion is forgotten. Write the units in the calculation: n = m/M = (1.0 × 10⁻⁶ g)/(131 g mol⁻¹) = 7.6 × 10⁻⁹ mol. The grams cancel only if both masses are in the same unit.

Working: N = (m/M)N_A = (1.0 × 10⁻⁶ g/131 g mol⁻¹) × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 4.60 × 10¹⁵ nuclei. T½ = 8.0 × 8.64 × 10⁴ s = 6.91 × 10⁵ s, so λ = ln 2/T½ = 0.693/(6.91 × 10⁵ s) = 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. A = λN = 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹ × 4.60 × 10¹⁵ = 4.6 × 10⁹ Bq.
items.specStatementText: the activity as the rate of decay as given by A = λN = λN₀e^(−λt)

items.q: Samples X and Y each contain 4.0 × 10¹⁸ undecayed nuclei. The nuclide in X has a half-life of 2.0 h; the nuclide in Y has a half-life of 8.0 h. Which statement about their activities at this instant is correct?
items.correct: X has four times the activity of Y, as its decay constant is four times larger.
items.misconception: Y has four times the activity of X, as its nuclei remain radioactive for longer.
items.why:
Long-lived nuclear waste is described as especially dangerous, so students link 'long half-life' with 'more radioactive' and do not separate how long a hazard lasts from how fast radiation is emitted. Activity is the number of decays per second. For N nuclei, A = (ln 2/T½)N: quadrupling the half-life quarters the activity. The hazard of long-lived waste comes from its emitting for a very long time, not from a high activity.

Working: A = λN and λ = ln 2/T½. λ_X = 0.693/2.0 h = 0.347 h⁻¹; λ_Y = 0.693/8.0 h = 0.0866 h⁻¹. With equal N, A_X/A_Y = λ_X/λ_Y = 8.0/2.0 = 4.
items.specStatementText: the activity as the rate of decay as given by A = λN = λN₀e^(−λt)
items.random_wrong: They have equal activities, as they contain equal numbers of nuclei still undecayed.

items.q: To determine the half-life of a nuclide, a student plots a graph of ln(corrected count rate) against time. The graph is a straight line with a gradient of −0.0231 min⁻¹. What is the half-life of the nuclide?
items.correct: 30 min
items.misconception: 13 min
items.why:
Calculators have 'log' and 'ln' keys side by side, and students who remember that 'a logarithm undoes an exponential' do not register that each logarithm undoes only its own base. ln is the logarithm to base e and is the one that undoes eˣ: ln(e^(−λt)) = −λt. log₁₀ undoes 10ˣ. Use ln with λ and e.

Working: For C = C₀e^(−λt), ln C = ln C₀ − λt, so the gradient is −λ and λ = 0.0231 min⁻¹. T½ = ln 2/λ = 0.693/0.0231 min⁻¹ = 30.0 min ≈ 30 min.
items.specStatementText: the relationship between half-life and the decay constant as given by T½ = ln2/λ.
items.random_wrong: 43 min
items.working: For C = C₀e^(−λt), ln C = ln C₀ − λt, so the gradient is −λ and λ = 0.0231 min⁻¹. T½ = ln 2/λ = 0.693/0.0231 min⁻¹ = 30.0 min ≈ 30 min.

items.q: Which pair are isotopes of the same element?
items.correct: ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl
items.misconception: ³¹₁₅P and ³²₁₆S
items.why: The definition is learned as 'same one, different other' and the two particles are swapped in memory. Neutrons feel like the 'variable' particle because textbooks say isotopes 'differ in the number of neutrons', and the fixed particle is forgotten. Fix the proton number first: Z decides the element, so isotopes must share Z. Then ask what differs: the neutron number N, and so the nucleon number A = Z + N. In ᴬ_ZX notation, isotopes have the same lower number and different upper numbers.
items.specStatementText: isotopes
items.random_wrong: ⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴⁰₁₉K

items.q: In the fusion reaction ²₁H + ²₁H → ³₂He + ¹₀n the rest masses are 1875.61 MeV c⁻² for ²₁H, 2808.39 MeV c⁻² for ³₂He and 939.57 MeV c⁻² for the neutron. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. How much energy is released in one reaction?
items.correct: 3.26 MeV
items.why:
The parent nucleus does lose about 4 u, and the α particle carries this mass away, so students identify 'mass lost by the parent' with 'mass converted into energy'. Compare total rest masses before and after: Δm = m(parent) − [m(daughter) + m(α)]. Nucleon number is conserved (226 = 222 + 4); only the tiny difference Δm appears as energy, E = Δmc².

Working: Rest mass of reactants = 2 × 1875.61 = 3751.22 MeV c⁻². Rest mass of products = 2808.39 + 939.57 = 3747.96 MeV c⁻². Δm = 3751.22 − 3747.96 = 3.26 MeV c⁻². E = Δmc² = 3.26 MeV c⁻² × c² = 3.26 MeV (the c² cancels; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ is not used numerically). Accepted value 3.27 MeV. Check: 3.26 MeV = 3.26 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J = 5.22 × 10⁻¹³ J, consistent with Δm = 3.26/931.5 u = 0.003500 u = 5.81 × 10⁻³⁰ kg and E = 5.81 × 10⁻³⁰ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 5.23 × 10⁻¹³ J.
items.specStatementText: the mass-energy equivalence as given by E = mc² in nuclear reactions

E = Δmc² = 3.26 MeV c⁻² × c² = 3.26 MeV (the c² cancels; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ is not used numerically). Accepted value 3.27 MeV. items.q: A helium-4 nucleus contains two protons and two neutrons. Between which pairs of particles does the strong nuclear force act?
items.correct: Between every pair of nucleons: proton–proton, neutron–neutron and proton–neutron.
items.misconception: Only between a proton and a neutron; two protons or two neutrons do not attract each other.
items.why: Textbooks often say that neutrons 'help hold the nucleus together', and students take this to mean that neutrons are the only source of the attraction. Every nucleon attracts its near neighbours through the strong force, whether they are protons or neutrons. The force between two protons is the sum of a strong attraction and an electric repulsion; at about 10⁻¹⁵ m the attraction is the larger.
items.specStatementText: the existence of the strong nuclear force, a short-range, attractive force between nucleons
items.random_wrong: Between every pair except the two protons, which repel each other as they carry like charges.

items.q: A nucleus emits a β⁺ particle, and the daughter nucleus then emits a γ photon. How do the proton number Z and neutron number N of the final nucleus compare with those of the original nucleus?
items.correct: Z is one less and N is one more.
items.misconception: Neither Z nor N has changed.
items.why:
Students know that electrons are found in shells outside the nucleus and that the nucleus contains only protons and neutrons, so an emitted electron seems to have to come from the shells. In β⁻ decay a neutron in the nucleus becomes a proton, and an electron and an antineutrino are created and emitted. The proton number rises by 1, so the element changes, and the nucleon number stays the same: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e + ⁰₀ν̄.

Working: β⁺ decay: p → n + e⁺ + ν, so Z → Z − 1, N → N + 1, A unchanged. γ emission: the excited daughter drops to a lower energy state; Z, N and A are all unchanged. Overall: Z − 1, N + 1.
items.specStatementText: the changes in the state of the nucleus following alpha, beta and gamma radioactive decay
items.random_wrong: Z is one more, and N is one less.
items.working: β⁺ decay: p → n + e⁺ + ν, so Z → Z − 1, N → N + 1, A unchanged. γ emission: the excited daughter drops to a lower energy state; Z, N and A are all unchanged. Overall: Z − 1, N + 1.

items.q: Fluorine-18, used in PET scanning, decays by β⁺ emission: ¹⁸₉F → ¹⁸₈O + e⁺ + X. What is the particle X?
items.correct: a neutrino, ν, from the nucleus
items.misconception: a γ photon emitted by the nucleus
items.why: Both are uncharged, both carry energy away from a decaying nucleus, and both are described as having no or almost no mass, so students merge them. Distinguish them by origin and behaviour: γ photons come from an excited nucleus dropping to a lower energy state and are absorbed by thick lead or concrete; neutrinos and antineutrinos are created in β decay and very rarely interact with anything.
items.specStatementText: the existence of neutrinos ν and antineutrinos ν̄
items.random_wrong: an antineutrino, ν̄, from the nucleus

items.q: With no radioactive source near it, a detector still records a count rate. Which statement about this background count rate is correct?
items.correct: It comes from cosmic rays and from radioactive nuclides in rock, air and buildings and is subtracted from each reading.
items.misconception: It is the same in every minute, so a single one-minute reading gives its value exactly and no repeat readings are needed.
items.why: 'Background' sounds like a steady hum, and worked examples state it as one tidy figure ('background = 30 counts min⁻¹'). Students do not connect it with the randomness of decay that they learn separately. Background counts come from random decays and random cosmic-ray arrivals, so they fluctuate like any radioactive count. Measure background for a long time (or repeat and average) and subtract the mean from every reading taken with the source.
items.specStatementText: the effect of background radiation on count rate.
items.random_wrong: It is radiation that has soaked into the detector from sources used earlier, and it fades once the detector is left unused.

items.q: The deuteron, ²₁H, is a stable nucleus made of one proton and one neutron; its binding energy is 2.2 MeV. The neutron carries no electric charge. Which conclusion do these facts support?
items.correct: An attractive force other than the electric force acts between a proton and a neutron.
items.misconception: The gravitational attraction between the two nucleons is strong enough to bind them together.
items.why: Students know that gravity increases as masses get closer and that gravity holds planets and stars together, so it is a natural candidate for the attraction in a nucleus. They do not estimate how small the masses of nucleons are. Estimate both forces for two protons in a nucleus: Gm²/r² ≈ 10⁻³⁵ N and ke²/r² ≈ 60 N. Gravity cannot balance the repulsion; a far stronger attraction between nucleons, the strong nuclear force, is needed.
items.specStatementText: the evidence for the strong nuclear force
items.random_wrong: The proton's electric field attracts the neutron, as it attracts the electron in a hydrogen atom.

items.q: Light stable nuclides have roughly equal numbers of neutrons and protons, but heavy stable nuclides have many more neutrons than protons: ²⁰⁸₈₂Pb has N/Z ≈ 1.5. Why do heavy nuclei need this excess of neutrons to be stable?
items.correct: Extra neutrons add strong-force attraction, which acts only between near neighbours, without adding electric repulsion, which acts between every pair of protons.
items.misconception: The neutrons sit between the protons and shield them from one another's electric repulsion, so more protons need more neutrons between them.
items.why: Students know neutrons are uncharged and that heavy nuclei need more of them, and reach for a familiar picture: an uncharged material placed between charges as a barrier, like insulation. The real reason, more attraction with no extra repulsion, is never stated in those terms. The electric force acts between every pair of protons regardless of what is between them, and grows with the number of proton pairs. Extra neutrons add short-range strong attraction to their neighbours and no repulsion, tipping the balance back towards binding.
items.specStatementText: the role of the ratio of neutrons to protons for the stability of nuclides
items.random_wrong: The strong force acts only between a proton and a neutron, so each proton must be surrounded by more than one neutron to be held in place.

items.q: The binding energy per nucleon peaks at 8.8 MeV for ⁵⁶₂₆Fe and is roughly constant above a nucleon number of about 60, falling slowly to 7.9 MeV for ²⁰⁸₈₂Pb. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The total binding energy of lead-208 is about 3.3 times that of iron-56, though each nucleon in it is less tightly bound.
items.misconception: The total binding energy of iron-56 is greater than that of lead-208, since its binding energy per nucleon is greater.
items.why:
Both quantities are called 'binding energy' in conversation and appear side by side in tables and graphs. Students remember that 'more binding energy means more stable' and drop the words 'per nucleon'. To compare how tightly nuclei are bound, divide the total binding energy by the nucleon number. The binding energy curve plots binding energy per nucleon, and the nuclei near its peak are the most tightly bound. Energy is released when nuclei change into nuclei with a greater binding energy per nucleon.

Working: Total binding energy E_b = (E_b/A) × A. Lead-208: 7.9 MeV × 208 = 1643 MeV ≈ 1.6 × 10³ MeV. Iron-56: 8.8 MeV × 56 = 492.8 MeV ≈ 4.9 × 10² MeV. Ratio = 1643/492.8 = 3.33 ≈ 3.3. (If E_b grew as A², the ratio would be (208/56)² = 13.8 ≈ 14.)
items.specStatementText: the approximate constancy of binding energy curve above a nucleon number of 60
items.random_wrong: The total binding energy of lead-208 is about 14 times that of iron-56, since every nucleon in it attracts every other nucleon.
items.working: Total binding energy E_b = (E_b/A) × A. Lead-208: 7.9 MeV × 208 = 1643 MeV ≈ 1.6 × 10³ MeV. Iron-56: 8.8 MeV × 56 = 492.8 MeV ≈ 4.9 × 10² MeV. Ratio = 1643/492.8 = 3.33 ≈ 3.3. (If E_b grew as A², the ratio would be (208/56)² = 13.8 ≈ 14.)

items.q: Thorium-228 decays by α emission to radium-224, which has an excited state 0.08 MeV above its ground state. The α particles emitted when radium-224 is formed in its ground state have kinetic energy 5.42 MeV. Ignoring the recoil of the radium nucleus, which statement about the α particles emitted when radium-224 is formed in its excited state is correct?
items.correct: They have kinetic energy 5.34 MeV, and a 0.08 MeV γ photon is emitted as the radium nucleus falls to its ground state.
items.misconception: They have kinetic energy 5.50 MeV, as they carry the extra 0.08 MeV that the excited radium nucleus possesses.
items.why:
'Excited' is heard as 'more energy in the decay', and the extra energy is attached to the particle that leaves. The fixed total energy released, which must be shared between α, recoil and excitation, is not part of the student's picture. Start from the fixed energy released. Excitation energy retained by the daughter is subtracted from what the α particle can take: E_α ≈ E_released − E_excitation. The excited daughter later emits that energy as a γ photon.

Working: Energy released is the same in every decay of thorium-228 to radium-224. Ground-state decay: E_α = 5.42 MeV (recoil ignored). Decay to the excited state: the daughter retains 0.08 MeV, so E_α = 5.42 − 0.08 = 5.34 MeV. The excited radium-224 nucleus then emits a γ photon of energy 0.08 MeV. (Measured values: α energies 5.423 MeV and 5.340 MeV; γ energy 0.084 MeV.)
items.specStatementText: that the spectrum of alpha and gamma radiations provides evidence for discrete nuclear energy levels
items.random_wrong: They also have kinetic energy 5.42 MeV, because a given nuclide emits α particles of a single energy only.
items.working: Energy released is the same in every decay of thorium-228 to radium-224. Ground-state decay: E_α = 5.42 MeV (recoil ignored). Decay to the excited state: the daughter retains 0.08 MeV, so E_α = 5.42 − 0.08 = 5.34 MeV. The excited radium-224 nucleus then emits a γ photon of energy 0.08 MeV. (Measured values: α energies 5.423 MeV and 5.340 MeV; γ energy 0.084 MeV.)

items.q: The α particles from a given decay to the daughter's ground state all have the same kinetic energy, whereas the β⁻ particles from a given decay have a continuous range of kinetic energies up to a maximum. Which statement correctly explains this difference?
items.correct: α decay produces two bodies, so conservation of momentum fixes the α particle's share of the energy; β⁻ decay produces three, so the electron's share can vary.
items.misconception: Every α decay of a nuclide releases exactly the same energy, but the energy released varies from one β⁻ decay to the next, so the electron's energy varies with it.
items.why: A continuous spectrum is often read directly as evidence of continuous energy states, which is correct for some spectra (for example that of a hot solid), so students apply the same inference here. Compare with α decay: discrete α and γ energies show discrete nuclear levels. With discrete levels and a fixed decay energy, a continuous β spectrum can only mean that another particle shares the energy.
items.specStatementText: the continuous spectrum of beta decay as evidence for the neutrino
items.random_wrong: Both kinds of particle leave the nucleus with a single energy, but β⁻ particles lose varying amounts of energy in collisions before they escape the source.

items.q: A sample contains 8.0 × 10²⁰ nuclei of iodine-131, which has a half-life of 8.0 days. How many iodine-131 nuclei remain after 20 days?
items.why:
At standard level all examples use whole half-lives, so the halving sequence becomes the only tool. When a time does not divide exactly, the student forces it to, rather than using the exponential law. For any time t use N = N₀e^(−λt) with λ = ln 2/T½, or equivalently N = N₀(½)^(t/T½) with a non-integer exponent. Check against the halving sequence: after 2.5 half-lives the answer must lie between the values for 2 and 3 half-lives.

Working: λ = ln 2/T½ = 0.6931/8.0 days = 0.08664 day⁻¹. λt = 0.08664 day⁻¹ × 20 days = 1.733. N = N₀e^(−λt) = 8.0 × 10²⁰ × e^(−1.733) = 8.0 × 10²⁰ × 0.1768 = 1.41 × 10²⁰ ≈ 1.4 × 10²⁰. Equivalently N = N₀(½)^(20/8.0) = N₀(½)^2.5 = N₀/5.66.
items.specStatementText: the decay constant λ and the radioactive decay law as given by N = N₀e^(−λt)

items.q: The decay constant λ of a nuclide has the unit s⁻¹. Which statement about λ is correct?
items.correct: The probability that a nucleus decays in a short time Δt is approximately λΔt, provided λΔt is much less than one.
items.misconception: The probability that a nucleus decays in a short time interval is approximately equal to λ, provided the interval is short.
items.why: 'λ is the probability of decay' is remembered without the words 'per unit time', so λ is treated as a pure number and its unit is ignored. Check units: a probability has no unit, but λ is in s⁻¹. λ becomes a probability only when multiplied by a time: λΔt for a short interval, or through 1 − e^(−λt) in general.
items.specStatementText: that the decay constant approximates the probability of decay in unit time only in the limit of sufficiently small λt
items.random_wrong: The probability that a nucleus decays within a time t is exactly λt, however long the interval t may be.

items.q: Technetium-99m, used in medical imaging, has a half-life of 6.0 h. What is its decay constant?
items.why:
Half-lives are quoted in whatever unit is convenient and λ is computed from them without units being carried. Because λ 'is a constant', the student does not expect it to change when the time unit changes. λ has the unit of 1/time and its value changes with the unit: 0.12 h⁻¹ = 0.12/3600 s⁻¹ = 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹. Convert T½ to the required time unit before dividing, or convert λ afterwards, and always write the unit on λ.

Working: T½ = 6.0 h × 3600 s h⁻¹ = 2.16 × 10⁴ s. λ = ln 2/T½ = 0.6931/(2.16 × 10⁴ s) = 3.21 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ ≈ 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹. (In hours: λ = 0.6931/6.0 h = 0.116 h⁻¹; 0.116/3600 = 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹, consistent.)
items.specStatementText: the relationship between half-life and the decay constant as given by T½ = ln2/λ.

items.q: Do isotopes of an element have different chemical properties?
items.correct: No. Chemical behaviour is set by the electrons, and a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons. All isotopes of an element have the same proton number, so they have the same chemical properties; they differ in mass and in nuclear properties such as stability.
items.misconception: Isotopes have different nuclei, so they have different chemical properties and could be separated by chemical reactions.
items.why: Isotopes are described as 'different forms' of an element, and radioactive isotopes clearly behave differently from stable ones, so students extend the difference to chemistry. The idea that chemistry depends on electrons, not on the whole nucleus, is not connected to isotopes. The chemical properties of an atom depend on its electrons. Isotopes of an element have the same number of electrons in the neutral atom, so they react in the same way. This is why a radioactive isotope such as iodine-131 is taken up by the body exactly as stable iodine is.
items.specStatementText: isotopes

items.q: Are isotopes atoms of an element with different numbers of electrons?
items.correct: No. Atoms of an element with different numbers of electrons are ions. Isotopes are nuclides with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
items.misconception: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have gained or lost electrons, so they have the same nucleus but different numbers of electrons.
items.why: Isotopes and ions are both introduced as 'versions' of an atom of one element, often in the same lesson, and each involves a change in the number of one kind of particle. Students remember that a particle number changes but not which particle. An ion differs from its atom in the number of electrons; isotopes of an element differ from each other in the number of neutrons in the nucleus. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons (and 6 electrons when neutral); carbon-12 has 6 neutrons and carbon-14 has 8.
items.specStatementText: isotopes
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a nucleus have more mass than the separate protons and neutrons that make it up?
items.correct: No. The mass of a nucleus is LESS than the total mass of its separated nucleons. The difference is the mass defect, and the mass defect multiplied by c² is the binding energy.
items.misconception: A nucleus has more mass than its separate nucleons, because binding them together adds something, the 'glue' that holds them, to the mass.
items.why: In everyday life, joining parts together never reduces the total mass, and in chemistry students learn that mass is conserved. The idea that something 'holds' the nucleus together suggests that the nucleus contains something extra. When nucleons bind, energy is released, and by mass–energy equivalence the system loses mass: Δm = E_b/c². So m_nucleus < Z m_p + (A − Z) m_n, and the mass defect Z m_p + (A − Z) m_n − m_nucleus is positive for every bound nucleus.
items.specStatementText: nuclear binding energy and mass defect
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the energy released in a nuclear reaction equal to the total binding energy of the products?
items.correct: No. The energy released equals the total binding energy of the products MINUS the total binding energy of the reactants. The reactants were already bound, so only the increase in binding energy is released.
items.misconception: The energy released in fusion or fission is the binding energy of the nucleus or nuclei formed, because binding energy is released when a nucleus forms.
items.why: Students correctly learn that energy is released when nucleons bind to form a nucleus, then apply this to the products only, forgetting that the reacting nuclei were already bound. Picture the reactants being separated into nucleons (this needs their total binding energy) and the nucleons then combining into the products (this releases the products' total binding energy). The net energy released is BE(products) − BE(reactants).
items.specStatementText: the variation of the binding energy per nucleon with nucleon number
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the energy released be found by subtracting the binding energies per nucleon of the reactants from that of the products?
items.correct: No. Each binding energy per nucleon must first be multiplied by the nucleon number of its nucleus to give the total binding energy. The energy released is the difference between the TOTAL binding energies of products and reactants.
items.misconception: The energy released in a nuclear reaction is the binding energy per nucleon of the products minus the binding energies per nucleon of the reactants.
items.why: Binding energy curves and data tables give binding energy per nucleon, and students substitute these values directly into 'products minus reactants' without converting them to totals. Convert each value to a total, A × (binding energy per nucleon), then subtract. For ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + n: 4(7.07) − [2(1.11) + 3(2.83)] = 17.6 MeV, not 7.07 − 1.11 − 2.83 = 3.13 MeV.
items.specStatementText: the variation of the binding energy per nucleon with nucleon number

items.q: Is 1 MeV equal to 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J?
items.correct: No. 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so 1 MeV = 10⁶ eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J.
items.misconception: An energy in MeV is converted to joules by multiplying by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹, as for an energy in electronvolts; the prefix 'mega' can be ignored.
items.why: Students memorize 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J as the conversion for the electronvolt and apply it to any unit containing 'eV', overlooking the prefix. Deal with the prefix first: 1 MeV = 1 × 10⁶ eV = 1 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J.
items.specStatementText: the mass-energy equivalence as given by E = mc² in nuclear reactions

items.q: Do the electrons around a nucleus block the strong nuclear force from reaching other nuclei?
items.correct: No. Nothing blocks the strong force; it simply becomes negligible at separations much greater than about 10⁻¹⁵ m. Neighbouring nuclei in a solid are about 10⁻¹⁰ m apart, far beyond its range.
items.misconception: The electrons around each nucleus shield neighbouring nuclei from its strong nuclear force.
items.why: Students meet shielding for radiation (lead blocks γ rays) and for electric fields, and many believe that material in the way can block forces in general, as in the common idea that there is no gravity where there is no air. They apply the same picture to the strong force. The strong force is short-range: large at about 10⁻¹⁵ m and negligible a few times further out. It does not need to be blocked; it does not reach from one nucleus to the next.
items.specStatementText: the existence of the strong nuclear force, a short-range, attractive force between nucleons

items.q: Because decay is random, does that mean that the half-life of a sample cannot be measured or predicted?
items.correct: No. Randomness applies to individual nuclei: we cannot say when a particular nucleus will decay. For a large number of nuclei the fraction that decays in a given time is highly predictable, which is why each nuclide has a definite half-life.
items.misconception: Because radioactive decay is random, the behaviour of a whole sample is unpredictable, so its half-life cannot be measured and samples cannot be compared.
items.why: In everyday language 'random' means 'without any pattern'. Students see the count rate jump about from one reading to the next and conclude that there is no regularity at all. Random means that the timing of each individual decay is unpredictable. With very large numbers of nuclei the overall decay is highly predictable: half of a large sample decays in one half-life. Fluctuations in the count rate are reduced by counting for longer.
items.specStatementText: the random and spontaneous nature of radioactive decay
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does each undecayed nucleus become less likely to decay as a sample gets older and its activity falls?
items.correct: No. The activity falls because there are fewer undecayed nuclei left, not because each nucleus becomes less likely to decay. Every remaining nucleus has the same chance, ½, of decaying within the next half-life.
items.misconception: As a sample decays and its activity falls, each remaining nucleus becomes less likely to decay, so the chance of decay halves with every half-life.
items.why: Students attribute a property of the whole sample (its falling activity) to each nucleus in it, a common error when reasoning about populations and chance. Separate the sample from the nucleus. The activity depends on how many undecayed nuclei there are, and that number halves every half-life. The chance that any one undecayed nucleus decays within the next half-life is ½, however much time has passed.
items.specStatementText: the random and spontaneous nature of radioactive decay
