items.q: Does γ emission change the proton number or the nucleon number of a nucleus?
items.correct: No. γ emission takes a nucleus from an excited state to a lower energy state of the same nuclide. Z and A are both unchanged; only the energy of the nucleus decreases.
items.misconception: γ emission changes the nucleus as α and β emission do: it changes the proton number or the nucleon number, producing a different nuclide.
items.why: γ radiation is taught with α and β as one of 'the three types of radioactive decay', and the other two both transform the nucleus, so students assume that all three do. A γ photon has no charge and no nucleon number: ⁹⁹ᵐ₄₃Tc → ⁹⁹₄₃Tc + γ. The nucleus is the same nuclide before and after; it has only lost energy. γ emission usually follows an α or β decay that has left the daughter nucleus in an excited state.
items.specStatementText: the changes in the state of the nucleus following alpha, beta and gamma radioactive decay
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the antineutrino carry a charge opposite to that of the β⁻ particle?
items.correct: No. Both the neutrino and the antineutrino are uncharged. Charge in β⁻ decay balances without them: 0 → (+1) + (−1).
items.misconception: The antineutrino emitted in β⁻ decay is positively charged, because an antiparticle has the opposite charge and it balances the charge of the β⁻ particle.
items.why: The first antiparticle students meet is the positron, whose charge is opposite to the electron's, so 'anti' is taken to mean 'opposite charge'. Seeing the antineutrino next to the electron in the equation suggests it cancels the electron's charge. An antiparticle has the opposite charge to its particle only if the particle is charged. The neutrino is uncharged, so the antineutrino is uncharged too. In n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ the charges are 0 = (+1) + (−1) + 0.
items.specStatementText: the existence of neutrinos ν and antineutrinos ν̄
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the least ionizing radiation the least hazardous in every situation?
items.correct: No. γ rays are weakly ionizing but so penetrating that a γ source outside the body irradiates internal organs, whereas α particles from a source outside the body are stopped by the dead outer layer of skin. The hazard depends on where the source is as well as on the type of radiation.
items.misconception: γ rays are the safest radiation to be near, because they are the least ionizing.
items.why: Students learn that ionization is what damages cells and rank hazard by ionizing ability alone, forgetting that radiation must reach living cells before it can ionize them. Consider ionization and penetration together. Outside the body, α is the least hazardous and β and γ are more hazardous because they reach living tissue; inside the body, α is the most hazardous because all its energy is deposited in nearby cells.
items.specStatementText: the penetration and ionizing ability of alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does radiation stay behind in an object after the source has been removed?
items.correct: No. Radiation is emitted by a source and is absorbed very soon after being emitted. When the source is removed, no radiation remains; only radioactive material, if any has been left behind, can keep emitting.
items.misconception: Radiation is a kind of substance that can soak into, collect in, or be trapped inside objects and stay there after the source has been taken away.
items.why: Research on students' ideas about radioactivity reports that radiation is often pictured as an invisible substance rather than as particles or photons travelling from a source. News language about radiation 'leaking' or 'spreading' encourages the picture. α and β particles and γ photons travel away from the source and are absorbed, giving up their energy; they do not accumulate. What can persist is radioactive MATERIAL (contamination), which keeps emitting radiation.
items.specStatementText: the penetration and ionizing ability of alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the mass of a radioactive sample halve in one half-life?
items.correct: No. Half of the radioactive NUCLEI decay, but they become daughter nuclei that stay in the sample if the daughter is a solid. The sample's mass hardly changes; only the emitted particles and a tiny amount of mass-energy leave.
items.misconception: In one half-life the sample loses half of its mass, because half of it has 'gone' by decaying.
items.why: Students picture decay as the material disappearing or evaporating, and attach the word 'half' to the whole sample rather than to the number of undecayed nuclei of the parent nuclide. Half-life refers to the number of undecayed nuclei of the parent nuclide, and so to the activity. When cobalt-60 decays it becomes nickel-60, a solid with almost the same mass, so the sample's mass stays almost constant while its cobalt-60 content halves.
items.specStatementText: the activity, count rate and half-life in radioactive decay
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a larger sample of a radioactive nuclide have a longer half-life?
items.correct: No. The half-life is a property of the nuclide and is the same for any size of sample. A larger sample has a greater activity, but its activity halves in the same time.
items.misconception: A larger sample takes longer to fall to half, because there is more of it to get through.
items.why: In everyday processes more material takes longer to use up (a larger pile of wood takes longer to burn). Research on students' ideas about half-life reports that many think the half-life depends on the amount of material. Each nucleus has the same chance of decaying in a given time, so the number decaying per second is proportional to the number present. Doubling the sample doubles the activity, and the same fraction decays in each half-life.
items.specStatementText: the activity, count rate and half-life in radioactive decay
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: After background has been subtracted, does the counter then read only the corrected count rate?
items.correct: No. The counter always records background as well as the source. Subtracting background is a step in a calculation; a prediction of what the counter will read must add the background back.
items.misconception: Once background has been measured and subtracted, it no longer affects the readings, so the counter will show only the corrected count rate.
items.why: Students treat 'correcting for background' as physically removing the background rather than as a step in the arithmetic. Measured count rate = count rate due to the source + background count rate. Use this relation both ways: subtract to analyse data, add to predict a reading.
items.specStatementText: the effect of background radiation on count rate.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a nuclide with too many neutrons decay by α emission to get rid of its extra neutrons?
items.correct: No. α emission removes two protons and two neutrons, which does not reduce the neutron excess of a light nucleus: for carbon-14 it would raise N/Z from 1.33 to 1.5. A neutron-rich nuclide decays by β⁻ emission, in which a neutron changes into a proton, lowering N/Z.
items.misconception: α decay is how a nucleus gets rid of surplus neutrons, since the α particle carries neutrons away.
items.why: Students know that α particles contain neutrons and that some nuclides have 'too many neutrons', and link the two without checking what happens to the ratio N/Z. Compare N/Z before and after. For ¹⁴₆C (N/Z = 8/6 = 1.33), α emission would give ¹⁰₄Be (N/Z = 6/4 = 1.5), which is worse; β⁻ emission gives ¹⁴₇N (N/Z = 1), which is stable. α decay is typical of very heavy nuclides, where it reduces the size of the nucleus.
items.specStatementText: the role of the ratio of neutrons to protons for the stability of nuclides
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the electric repulsion between protons negligible in large nuclei, because the strong force is so much stronger?
items.correct: No. The strong force acts only between near neighbours, but the electric repulsion acts between every pair of protons. In large nuclei the repulsion on each proton keeps growing, which is why the binding energy per nucleon falls slowly from about 8.8 MeV (A ≈ 56–62) to about 7.6 MeV (uranium) and why heavy nuclei need extra neutrons.
items.misconception: The strong nuclear force is so much stronger than the electric force that the repulsion between protons plays no part in the binding of large nuclei.
items.why: The strong force is introduced as 'the strongest force' and as the force that overcomes proton repulsion, so students conclude that the repulsion is always overwhelmed and can be ignored. Compare ranges: each nucleon is attracted only by its near neighbours, but each proton is repelled by every other proton in the nucleus. Adding protons increases the repulsion on each proton without increasing the strong-force attraction on it, so the binding energy per nucleon decreases for heavy nuclei.
items.specStatementText: the approximate constancy of binding energy curve above a nucleon number of 60
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are γ rays emitted by electrons moving between the energy levels of the atom?
items.correct: No. γ photons are emitted by the NUCLEUS when it moves from an excited nuclear energy level to a lower one. Their energies match differences between the α energies from the parent, which depend on the daughter nucleus, not on its electrons.
items.misconception: γ rays are produced in the same way as light: by electrons dropping between discrete energy levels of the atom.
items.why: The only discrete energy levels most students have met are the electron levels of atoms (in atomic spectra), and photons are remembered as 'what electrons emit when they drop a level'. Link the evidence: when α decay leaves the daughter nucleus with less energy in some decays than in others, the missing energy reappears as a γ photon of exactly that energy. The γ photon therefore comes from the nucleus changing between its own discrete energy levels.
items.specStatementText: that the spectrum of alpha and gamma radiations provides evidence for discrete nuclear energy levels
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is e^(−λt) the probability that a nucleus decays within time t?
items.correct: No. e^(−λt) = N/N₀ is the fraction of nuclei that have NOT decayed after time t, which is the probability that a given nucleus survives. The probability that it decays is 1 − e^(−λt).
items.misconception: The expression e^(−λt) from the decay law gives the probability that a nucleus decays within time t.
items.why: Students recognise e^(−λt) as 'the decay formula' and use it for any decay question without checking whether it describes the nuclei that have decayed or those that remain. N = N₀e^(−λt) gives the number REMAINING. The fraction decayed is 1 − N/N₀ = 1 − e^(−λt). Check at t = 0: nothing has decayed, and 1 − e⁰ = 0.
items.specStatementText: that the decay constant approximates the probability of decay in unit time only in the limit of sufficiently small λt
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do samples containing equal numbers of undecayed nuclei have equal activities, whatever the nuclide?
items.correct: No. Activity depends on the decay constant as well as on the number of nuclei: A = λN. Samples of different nuclides with equal N have activities in the ratio of their decay constants.
items.misconception: The activity of a sample depends only on how many radioactive nuclei it contains, so equal numbers of nuclei give equal activities whatever the nuclide.
items.why: Students first meet activity as proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei of one nuclide, and extend the proportionality to comparisons between different nuclides. Within one nuclide, A is proportional to N. Between nuclides, include λ: A = λN. A nuclide with a shorter half-life has a larger λ and so a larger activity for the same N.
items.specStatementText: the activity as the rate of decay as given by A = λN = λN₀e^(−λt)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: The rest masses in a reaction are given in MeV c⁻². Must the mass difference be multiplied by c² = 9.00 × 10¹⁶ m² s⁻² to find the energy released?
items.correct: No. A mass of 17.5 MeV c⁻² is defined as the mass whose energy equivalent is 17.5 MeV: E = mc² = 17.5 MeV c⁻² × c² = 17.5 MeV. The c² cancels algebraically; no numerical multiplication is needed.
items.misconception: A mass given in MeV c⁻² must still be multiplied by c² = 9.00 × 10¹⁶ m² s⁻² to find its energy equivalent, just as a mass in kg would be.
items.why: E = mc² is drilled with masses in kg, and the SI value of c² becomes part of the routine. The unit MeV c⁻² is read as a mass 'in MeV' that still needs the c² step, rather than as a unit built so that the c² cancels. Treat the unit as algebra: (MeV c⁻²) × c² = MeV. Multiply by 9.00 × 10¹⁶ only when the mass is in kg (giving joules); multiply by 931.5 MeV only when the mass is in u. A mass in MeV c⁻² converts to energy in MeV with no arithmetic at all.
items.specStatementText: the mass-energy equivalence as given by E = mc² in nuclear reactions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A mass difference of 17.5 MeV c⁻² is found in a fusion reaction. Is the energy released 17.5 × 931.5 MeV?
items.correct: No. The factor 931.5 MeV converts a mass in unified atomic mass units u to energy: 1 u = 931.5 MeV c⁻². A mass already in MeV c⁻² is 17.5 MeV of energy directly.
items.misconception: Every mass difference in a nuclear reaction must be multiplied by 931.5 to give the energy in MeV, whatever unit the masses were given in.
items.why: Almost every binding-energy example uses masses in u, so '× 931.5' becomes an automatic final step. The student does not check that the factor is a conversion from u, and applies it to masses in MeV c⁻² or kg. Write the conversion with its units: 1 u = 931.5 MeV c⁻². Multiply by 931.5 only if the mass is in u. If it is in MeV c⁻² the number is already the energy in MeV; if it is in kg use E = mc² with c in m s⁻¹ to get joules.
items.specStatementText: the mass-energy equivalence as given by E = mc² in nuclear reactions

items.q: Does the strong nuclear force act on the electrons of an atom as well as on the nucleons?
items.correct: No. The strong nuclear force acts only between nucleons (protons and neutrons). Electrons do not feel it at all; they are held in the atom by the electric attraction of the nucleus.
items.misconception: The strong nuclear force holds the whole atom together, so it acts on the electrons as well as on the protons and neutrons.
items.why: The force is introduced as 'the force that holds the atom together' in loose classroom language, and 'strong' suggests it dominates everything in the atom. Students merge the two separate bindings, nucleus and electron shells, into one. Separate the two bindings: nucleons are bound to each other by the strong nuclear force, which acts only between nucleons and only over about 10⁻¹⁵ m; electrons are bound to the nucleus by the electric force, over about 10⁻¹⁰ m. Electrons have no strong interaction.
items.specStatementText: the existence of the strong nuclear force, a short-range, attractive force between nucleons
